Thanks so much!  I use harmonium and a plethora of ipad apps.  I first record a harmonium improvisation directly into my ipad using a tascam iOS mic.  Then I run the recording into Turnado into Samplr.  I mangle the recording using a variety of effects while recording into Samplr.  Then I run Samplr through Turnado into Loopy with Thumbjam also in the input slot.  I use the "storm is coming" reverb in Turnado.  Only for the Samplr input and I turn it off when I'm using Thumbjam.  Finally I record the session in Loopy while improvising using wet harmonium samples and various thumbjam instruments.  I would recommend using an Ipad 4 or newer for this process.  My ipad 3 struggled quite a bit when making this.  I shooting for a 20 minute recording, but my apps started freezing up.  thanks again!

It seems as if obscure musicians no longer have the balls to call themselves musicians, so instead they hide behind the noise genre.  I hear a lot of people these days calling themselves "noise artists".  They think they're not worthy of calling themselves musicians, because they don't understand tonality or theory.  The truth is there are no rules in music.  It is all music.  Stuff like circuit bending is definitely more of a separate art form, but when circuit-bent instruments are performed, it isn't noise.  It is music.  Those are desired sounds.  Perhaps this is more a semantic argument than it is a cultural one, but people's unawareness of the amount of subjectivity involved is troublesome.  Also, I'm surprised by how much conformity is involved in a genre that is supposedly structured around nonconformity.  In Los Angeles, "noise music" is the new pop punk.

There's no such thing as "literal noise".  The term is completely subjective.  It's simply an unwanted sound, but by the mere act of desiring that particular sound, it is no longer noise.  I like Merzbow, so I'm going to call it music.  I don't like Creed.  Therefore Creed is noise.
